title: Essay on Shiny
text:
Shiny is an R package that allows you to build interactive web applications straight from R. It bridges the gap between complex data analysis and end-user accessibility.

No web dev skills needed: It builds the HTML, CSS, and Bootstrap framework for you behind the scenes.
Highly accessible: Users just need a web URL to interact with the dashboards.
Dynamic: It easily converts our standard static plots (like ggplot2) into interactive tools.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
Shiny is an R package created by Posit (formerly RStudio) that makes it easy to build interactive web applications directly from R. It was first introduced in 2012 as a way to help data professionals create dynamic applications without spending weeks or months learning web development. You do not need to know any HTML, CSS, or JavaScript to get started — if you can write R code, you can build a Shiny app.
The core value of Shiny is accessibility. Instead of sending a coworker a static PDF chart, you give them a URL. They open it in a browser, interact with the data themselves — filtering by year, adjusting sliders, selecting categories — and never have to look at a single line of code. Everything you already know how to do in R (data wrangling with tidyverse, visualization with ggplot2, statistical modeling) can be packaged into a live, shareable web app.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
Reactivity — The Magic Behind Shiny
Reactivity is the concept that makes Shiny feel alive. In a normal R script, code runs from top to bottom, once, and stops. In a Shiny app, the server is always listening.
Here is how the chain reaction works:

A user moves a slider or selects from a dropdown — the input changes.
The server detects which specific input changed.
Only the outputs that depend on that input are automatically re-run and updated on screen.

You do not need to tell Shiny when to update. It figures that out on its own based on which outputs reference which inputs. This is called a reactive context.
Code inside renderPlot(), renderTable(), and reactive() are all reactive — they re-execute automatically when their inputs change. Code outside of these functions (like loading data at the top of the server) only runs once when the app first starts.

⚠️ Common mistake: Trying to use input$variable outside of a reactive context will cause an error. Always wrap input references inside render* or reactive() functions.


Reactive Expressions
For more complex apps, you can use reactive() to create a reusable intermediate calculation that only re-runs when its inputs change:
server <- function(input, output) {
  
  # This filtered dataset re-runs only when input$year changes
  filtered_data <- reactive({
    coachella |> filter(year == input$year)
  })
  
  output$attendancePlot <- renderPlot({
    ggplot(filtered_data(), aes(x = headliner, y = attendance)) +
      geom_col()
  })
}
Using reactive() prevents the same computation from running multiple times if several outputs depend on the same filtered data.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
Deploying and Sharing Your App
An app that only runs on your laptop is not very useful. Once it works locally, you need to host it so others can access it via a URL.

Shinyapps.io (Recommended for Beginners)
Shinyapps.io is a cloud hosting service by Posit. You can publish your app with one click directly from RStudio using the rsconnect package. A free tier is available for getting started and is perfect for class projects or small internal tools.


Security Considerations
If your app contains sensitive company data, do not use the free public tier. Options for adding protection include:

shinymanager package — adds a username/password login screen to any existing Shiny app with just a few lines of code.
Private Shiny Server — host internally so the app never leaves your company network.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
Pro Tips Before You Start
Sketch first, code second. Before writing a single line, draw your app layout on paper. Decide where the filters go, what the main chart shows, and whether you need tabs or multiple pages. The fluidRow() and column() layout functions map directly to a grid — a sketch makes this much easier to organize.
Start small. Build the simplest possible version first — one input, one output. Get that working, then add complexity. It is much easier to debug a small app than a large one.
Keep UI and server names in sync. The most common beginner bug is a mismatch between the inputId in the UI and input$... in the server. Use clear, consistent names like input$selected_year, not input$x.
Load data outside the server function. Any data loading or package setup that doesn’t depend on user input should go above the ui and server definitions in app.R, so it only runs once when the app starts rather than every time a user interacts with the app.

title: Essay on Shinylive
text: Shinylive is a method for running Shiny applications entirely within the user’s web browser, no dedicated R server required. It achieves this using WebR, a version of R compiled to run directly in the browser. Instead of sending user inputs to a remote server and waiting for a response, the browser itself becomes the “server.”

2. Shinylive vs. Traditional Shiny
The fundamental difference is where the computation happens:








Feature
Traditional Shiny
Shinylive (Serverless)




Server Requirement
Needs a backend (Shiny Server, Posit Connect, etc.)
No backend needed, hosted as static files (e.g., GitHub Pages)


Computation
Happens on the remote server
Happens on the user’s local machine/browser


Cost
Can be expensive to maintain and scale
Extremely low cost, often free via static hosting


Scaling
Limited by server capacity; can crash under high traffic
Scales infinitely, every new user brings their own computing power

title: Essay on Shinylive
section: 3. The Pros and Cons of Shinylive
text:
3. The Pros and Cons of Shinylive
Like any tool, Shinylive involves trade-offs. It is important to evaluate these before choosing it for a project.

3.1. Advantages
Zero Server Costs: Since you only need to serve static HTML/JS files, you can host apps for free on services like GitHub Pages or Netlify.
Infinite Scalability: You do not have to worry about a traffic spike crashing your server. If 10,000 people visit the app at once, 10,000 browsers do the work independently.
Permanent Existence: These apps can live indefinitely because they do not depend on a subscription-based server being maintained.


3.2. Disadvantages
The “No Secrets” Rule: Because the entire app and all its data are sent to the user’s browser, there are no secrets. You cannot hide API keys, database passwords, or proprietary algorithms. If it is in the app, the user can find it.
Initial Load Time: The first time a user visits, their browser must download the R environment. This currently takes approximately 5–10 seconds.
Package Limitations: Not all R packages are compatible with Shinylive. Specifically, packages that rely on curl or system-level dependencies may not work in the browser environment.
Data Access: Connecting directly to a private database is difficult because the browser’s security model, this makes traditional database connections impractical.

title: Essay on Shinylive
section: 4. When to Use Shinylive vs. Traditional Shiny
text:
4. When to Use Shinylive vs. Traditional Shiny
Use Shinylive if:

You are building a public-facing dashboard with open-source data (e.g., an academic supplement or public portfolio project).
You want to avoid the cost and maintenance of a server.
Your app uses standard tidyverse or ggplot2 logic without complex system dependencies.

Stick to Traditional Shiny if:

You need to connect to a private database using secure credentials.
You are handling sensitive or proprietary data/code that must stay on a company server.
Your app requires heavy computation that would overwhelm a user’s browser.

title: Essay on Shiny
section: 2. The Core Architecture of a Shiny App
text:
2. The Core Architecture of a Shiny App
Every Shiny app is built on two primary components that communicate with each other. You can store these as a single app.R file, or separate them into ui.R and server.R for larger team projects.

2.1. The User Interface (UI)
The UI is the front-end skeleton. It dictates what the user sees, how the page is laid out, and how they interact with the tool.

Layouts: You define the structural grid here. You can use standard setups like fluidPage with a sidebarLayout (which splits the screen into a sidebar for controls and a main panel for the graph), or you can use the shinydashboard package to build highly professional, modular dashboards with headers, sidebars, and body tabs.
Inputs: These are the widgets the user plays with to change the data. Examples include:

selectInput: A dropdown menu.
textInput: A text entry box.
sliderInput: A sliding numeric scale.








ImportantCrucial Rule



Every input must be assigned a unique ID (e.g., inputId = "post_type") so the Server knows exactly what to listen to.



Outputs: This is where you tell the UI to reserve visual space for the final product (e.g., plotOutput, tableOutput, textOutput).



2.2. The Server (The Brains)
The server works behind the scenes to take the inputs, process the data, and generate the outputs.

The server is initialized as a function with three arguments: input, output, and session.
Input is Read-Only: The server can only listen to the user’s input; it cannot change it. To interact with an input you defined in the UI, you call it using input$your_id (e.g., input$post_type).
Rendering Outputs: When you generate a graph or table, it must be wrapped in a specific reactive context to be sent back to the UI, such as renderPlot for a ggplot or renderText for a dynamic title.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
3. The Magic of Reactivity
This is the most important concept to grasp. Shiny is built on declarative programming rather than standard imperative programming.
In a standard R script, order strictly matters. You tell the computer exactly what to do line-by-line. In Shiny, you teach the app how to react if and when an input changes.

Reactive Dependencies: If an output depends on a specific input, Shiny creates a “reactive dependency.” Whenever the user moves a slider, Shiny automatically knows to trace that input back, recalculate the specific block of code tied to it, and instantly update the visual output.
Reactive Expressions reactive({}): If you are filtering a large dataset before plotting it, you don’t want to rewrite the filtering code for every single plot. You can create a reactive expression that filters your dataset based on the user’s input, saves it as an intermediate reactive object, and then passes that clean data to your output elements.







Note



When calling a reactive dataframe in the server, you must use parentheses, e.g., filtered_data().

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
4. Best Practices for Workflow
When we are building out these tools for the team, we should follow a structured sequence:

Sketch it out: Before coding, literally draw the dashboard on a piece of paper. Decide where the inputs go and what the final visual should look like.
Load Data Outside Reactivity: Read in your main CSV files or establish your basic tidy data at the very top of the script (or in the global environment) so the app only has to load the heavy data once upon startup, rather than every time the user clicks a button.
Build the static visual first: Write your ggplot or data wrangling code normally. Ensure the logic works first, then simply replace your hardcoded filter variables with the Shiny input$... variables.

title: Essay on Shiny
text:
5. Deployment and Security
Once the app is built, it isn’t useful if it only lives locally on our IDEs.

Deployment: You can bundle the app and host it on the cloud using services like shinyapps.io or Posit Cloud. By clicking the “Publish” button, R packages up the environment and deploys it to a live web URL.
Security: If the dashboard contains sensitive operational metrics, you cannot leave the URL open to the public. For basic projects, the shinymanager package allows you to easily wrap your UI in a secure login screen, requiring a simple username and password to access the data.

library(tidyverse)
library(gt)

coachella <- read_csv("coachella.csv") |>
  mutate(
    year       = as.numeric(year),
    attendance = as.numeric(attendance),
    daily_avg  = as.numeric(daily_avg)
  )

latest <- coachella |> arrange(desc(year)) |> slice(1)
peak   <- coachella |> slice_max(attendance, n = 1)
